clinicalPearls: A genetically heterogeneous disorder of epiphyseal cartilage; dominant forms arise from variants in COMP, COL9A1/2/3 or MATN3, and a recessive form from DTDST/SLC26A2 (also causing club feet)
Presents in childhood with joint pain (especially hips and knees), stiffness, a waddling gait and mildly short or normal stature
Radiographs show small, irregular, fragmented or flattened epiphyses that ossify late, most evident at the hips, knees and ankles
The metaphyses and spine are relatively normal, distinguishing it from spondyloepiphyseal and metaphyseal dysplasias
Early-onset osteoarthritis, particularly of the hips, is the major long-term consequence
A crucial mimic is the epiphyseal dysgenesis of untreated congenital hypothyroidism, which must be excluded biochemically
COMP variants also cause pseudoachondroplasia, so MED sits on a phenotypic spectrum with it
reference.pathophysiology: Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia results from defects in structural proteins of the cartilage extracellular matrix, most commonly cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP), type IX collagen or matrilin-3. Mutant proteins misfold and are retained within chondrocytes, causing endoplasmic reticulum stress and impaired secretion of a properly organised matrix. This preferentially disturbs the epiphyseal (articular and growth) cartilage, producing delayed and irregular epiphyseal ossification. The resulting incongruent, poorly formed joint surfaces predispose to premature degenerative osteoarthritis.
additionalDifferentials: Bilateral Perthes disease (avascular necrosis of the hips)
Meyer dysplasia of the femoral head
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey demonstrating symmetrical epiphyseal irregularity with normal metaphyses and spine
Thyroid function tests to exclude hypothyroid epiphyseal dysgenesis
Molecular genetic testing (COMP, COL9A1/2/3, MATN3, SLC26A2)
Hip and knee imaging to assess joint congruity and early osteoarthritic change
Assessment of feet and family members, particularly for the recessive SLC26A2 form
redFlags: Progressive hip pain and stiffness heralding early osteoarthritis needing orthopaedic input
Bilateral symmetrical femoral head changes that could be mistaken for Perthes disease
Untreated hypothyroidism as a reversible mimic with wider developmental consequences
Significant functional limitation or joint deformity in a growing child
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal and stature is often only mildly reduced, but premature osteoarthritis, especially of the hips, is common and may lead to joint replacement in adulthood.
pitfalls: Failing to check thyroid function and missing treatable hypothyroid epiphyseal dysgenesis
Misdiagnosing symmetrical hip changes as bilateral Perthes disease
Overlooking the milder end of the pseudoachondroplasia spectrum
Not counselling about recessive versus dominant inheritance depending on the causative gene
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: No disease-modifying drug therapy exists; care centres on protecting joints and preserving function through physiotherapy and activity modification to reduce load on the hips and knees
Analgesia for joint pain using simple analgesics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents for symptomatic osteoarthritis
Weight management and low-impact exercise to limit accelerated wear of incongruent joint surfaces
Orthopaedic surgery for symptomatic deformity or early osteoarthritis, including realignment osteotomy and eventual joint (particularly hip) replacement
Exclude and biochemically treat coexisting hypothyroidism, since untreated congenital hypothyroidism mimics the epiphyseal changes
Radiographic monitoring of the hips and knees for progressive joint incongruity and degenerative change
Genetic counselling for the dominant (COMP, COL9A, MATN3) and recessive (SLC26A2) forms, with clinical assessment of relatives
